Time
TīM
n. (in the Authorized Version rendering chiefly Hebrew 'ēth and mō'ēd, and Greek chronos (duration) and kairos (the appointed season))
From Old English tīma, a limited space of duration, cognate with Old Norse tīmi and ultimately with tide — that which is measured out, portioned, allotted. The root sense is not bare succession but allotment: a stretch of duration cut off and given. That is precisely the biblical sense. Scripture has no word for abstract empty time flowing on of itself; it speaks of times that are given, appointed, fulfilled, and ended. The Greek makes the distinction the English blurs: chronos is duration measured, kairos is the fit and appointed moment, and the Authorized Version renders both by this one word.

Biblical Definition

Time is the creature's measure, made by God when He made the world, and wholly under His government. It is not a vessel God inhabits but a thing He ordained: the lights were set in the firmament “for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years,” and duration itself began when the heaven and the earth began. God Himself is eternal, without succession, inhabiting eternity; He does not wait, and nothing overtakes Him. But everything He has made lives under measure, and that measure is His. The Preacher lays down the rule — “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecc 3:1) — and the appointed purpose is God's, not the creature's. David draws the pastoral comfort out of it in four words: “My times are in thy hand” (Psa 31:15). Not his time, but his times — the plural of every allotted season of a life, each one held. The redemptive centre of the doctrine is Gal 4:4: the Son was sent not early and not late but when the fulness of the time was come, which means the whole calendar of empires, exiles, and generations was a clock running to one hour. And because the days are evil, the believer is commanded to buy up the time (Eph 5:16) — to treat it as a purchased commodity, spent on account before God.

Webster 1828 Definition

A limited portion of duration, measured out and allotted by the Creator; in Scripture never bare succession but a season given, appointed, filled, and ended by God, in whose hand every creature's times are held.

expand to see more

TIME, n. 1. A particular portion or part of duration, whether past, present or future. The time was; the time has been; the time is; the time will be. Lo, the time is at hand.

2. A proper time; a season. There is a time to every purpose under heaven. Ecclesiastes 3. Webster's second sense is the biblical one: not duration in the abstract, but the fit and appointed occasion.

3. Duration. God, whose eternal duration is not to be measured, is said to inhabit eternity; time is the measure of things that begin and end, and therefore of the creature only.

4. A season; the state of things at a particular period. The times are evil. Hence the apostolic charge to redeem the time, that is, to buy it up as a merchant buys goods at market, because the season of opportunity is short.

5. Repetition of anything, or mention with reference to repetition. Four times; ten times. From this comes the common reckoning of times and half a time in the prophets, where a set and bounded period is intended.

Key Scripture

Ecclesiastes 3:1 — "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:"

Psalm 31:15 — "My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me."

Ephesians 5:16 — "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil."

Galatians 4:4 — "But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,"

Modern Corruption

Modern thought empties time of appointment and leaves only succession — a blind river carrying men nowhere — and then, having removed the Appointer, tells the creature that the moment belongs to him and must be seized before it is gone.

expand to see more

The governing modern assumption is that time is autonomous: an empty container running on by itself, indifferent to purpose, in which things merely happen. Strip the doctrine of providence out of duration and two errors follow at once. The first is fatalism — if the river carries everything and no one steers it, then nothing that happens means anything, which is the settled despair beneath a great deal of contemporary art and manner. The second is its mirror, the frantic self-assertion of carpe diem: if no one has appointed my season, I must seize it myself, and every hour not spent on my own advancement is an hour lost. Scripture cuts under both. The times are appointed, and they are appointed by a Person, and that Person is a Father to His people.

There is a second and subtler corruption inside the church — the treatment of one's own remaining time as an assumed possession. The rich fool did not deny God; he simply spoke of many years he had not been given (Luk 12:20), and that presumption was reckoned folly on the night it was answered. James names the same sin in ordinary speech: to say we will go into such a city and continue there a year, when we know not what shall be on the morrow, is to boast. The remedy is not anxiety but reckoning — asking God to teach us to number our days, so that the hours are spent as what they are, borrowed and accountable.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'ēth is the general word for a season or occasion; mō'ēd is the set time, the appointed meeting, from which the feasts take their name. Greek divides duration (chronos) from the fit moment (kairos), and the New Testament's decisive statements about redemption use the second.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'ēth (H6256) — time, season, occasion; the ordinary word, used of the time of harvest, the time of rain, the time of the singing of birds. Some 296 occurrences.

Hebrew mō'ēd (H4150) — an appointed time, a set feast, a place or time of meeting; the root of the tabernacle's name, the tent of meeting. Time as summons rather than as duration.

Hebrew yōm (H3117) — day; frequently rendered time where a period rather than a solar day is meant, as in “in the days of Noah.”

Greek chronos (G5550) — duration, extent of time, the quantity that clocks measure; the source of English chronology. Used of the times and seasons the Father has put in His own power (Act 1:7).

Greek kairos (G2540) — the fit, decisive, opportune moment; the season ripe for action. This is the word behind the command to redeem the time, and behind the Lord's statement that His time was not yet come.

Usage

"Of the appointed hour of redemption: the fulness of the time (Gal 4:4), the due time (Rom 5:6), the accepted time (2Co 6:2) — all of one determinate, sovereign appointment."

"Of a bounded prophetic period: a time, times, and the dividing of time (Dan 7:25; Rev 12:14), where the word denotes a set and limited term, not an indefinite stretch."

"Of the creature's allotment under providence: “My times are in thy hand” (Psa 31:15); “his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee” (Job 14:5)."
